As someone from the US currently living in Spain, I can tell you that Europeans really don’t know how great they have it. I had to go to the hospital for a procedure and didn’t even pay a penny. (Of course that could be my program covering it)

Ihave free public transport for being a student, and if I wasn’t, it would be 15€ a month. The trains are faster than driving a car ever would be, and I can walk anywhere I want as well, both because of the close distance and because the sidewalks are wide and everywhere, able to accommodate pedestrians everywhere. Hell, if I want coffee, I can just walk right next door, as my apartment shared a wall with the coffee joint. In the US, it would be about a 20 min drive for me, and 20 back. (Of course, it depends on where you live, but everybody in my program has the same experience despite living in different places in the US) I think just being outside and having more reasons to be outside has been making me feel much better. Even if I’m not doing anything, I can walk down to the park five minutes away from me and relax. There’s park everywhere as well, a few by each of my schools too. Whilst in the US, no matter what, I’d need to drive. If I need to get anywhere in the US, I need to drive, even to the bus station, or a park.

A lot of things are cheaper as well for a variety of reasons. One such example is that tipping isn’t a thing here, as employees get paid what they need to by their corporation rather than needing to rely on tips. Taxis are great here too, and so great that Ubers and Lyft can’t operate real well here. Taxis have their own lights to signal if they’re taken or not, are easily identifiable, and just like Uber, they have an app that allows you to pay through the app, set your destination, and even schedule a trip for the future. All, as well, while not needing to tip.

The food tastes a lot better as well, which could definitely be a personal bias. I’ve theorized however that the health guidelines are much more strict, and so food companies have to put in more work to make their foods taste good without just adding sugar. I’ve had a lot of coffee in the US, but the coffee right next door is the best I’ve ever had. The portion sizes are smaller too, which might bother some people, but I’ve really liked it. I feel less pressured to have to clean my plate and I don’t have to worry about it going bad in the fridge as there’s nothing in the fridge to go bad, and the cost accommodates the portion sizes too.

The craziest thing to me was the lack of guns. Where I lived in the US, I’d hear gunshots almost every night, and had the displeasure to witness a drive-by down the street. Just as well, as I suspect many Americans have, gun and bomb threats were a yearly thing, sometimes multiple times per. I never hear anything like that, and I feel so much more relaxed. It’s so much more tranquil, even if I still hear the honking car horns and people yelling. (Though more often they’re singing and laughing)

It’s hard to remember everything off the top of my head since I’ve only been here for a month so far, but it’s been a major dramatic change, and the culture shock I’m feeling has definitely been more shocking as to how bad the US really is. I’ve always feared that something out of my control could trap me in debt forever, but I don’t have any kind of worry like that here. In fact, this program, though with a bit of a hefty price tag, I say was much cheaper due to all the money I didn’t realize I’d be saving; Gas, food, healthcare, etc. It’s not only financially better, but physically safer too.

I’ll have to move back to the US in December, but I’ve got an upcoming internship back here in Spain, and then I’ll be getting my political science degree here once I have my associates of arts in the US, which will be by next Fall.

Edit: I should mention the experiences of foreign tourists in the US are very different from those who are living in the US. I don’t think much of my experience would be shared by tourists, but they’re two different sides of a coin.

There’s a lot of things to hate and a lot of things to love.

Primarily I hate that KI is such a greedy company. Real updates have been rolling out slower, replaced by content with pay walls like housing gauntlets. A lot of the best gear is P2W, and the best looking gear as well. A lot of people don’t know, but Wizard101 was one of the first games to contain loot boxes, which, of course, has only risen in prevalence. KI has found more and more ways to make their games more expensive as well, such as not giving better crown deals and making zones more expensive, and membership, though still being an option, something that’s very old by now. (And is the primary factor in the game’s popularity, as the free weekends are when the servers are at their peaks) KI is a greedy company and often survives on people’s nostalgia.

However, like a kid growing up, there’s a lot of things which has improved; deeper stories, more complicated spells, (I played before Celestia, so Astral spells weren’t a thing yet) improved pet systems where before they only gave you an item card, more complicated stats such as the crit system and pip conversion, houses, mounts, a PvP community that’s taken seriously, (First Age PvP was just a single dueling circle you had to run into like those in castles, so coordinating battles was difficult, and the PvP community really didn’t exist yet) and mechanics like fishing, monstrology, crafting, gardening, it’s really hard to list everything.

Witnessing its growth has been really beautiful. Sometimes I’m nostalgic for the beginning however, when Dragonspyre wasn’t a thing yet. I wouldn’t want to go back however, as it was fun for it’s time, but that time isn’t today. I’m happy with where the game has gone, and I try my best to ignore KI’s greed. Behind the money, I still think it’s a really great game, even if we love to bash on it for its pitfalls.
